blueprint_transcription: Farrell, H., & Newman, A. L. (2019). Weaponized interdependence: How global economic networks shape state coercion. International Security, 44(1), 42–79. https://doi.org/10.1 162/isec_a_00351. Contribution: Foundational network-topology/chokepoint concept. Difference: Does not deliver this paper's joint industrial project-level forecasts and adaptation-conditioned feedback equilibrium. Use: theoretical introduction and precise novelty boundary.

Clayton, C., Maggiori, M., & Schreger, J. (2024; revised April 2025). A theory of economic coercion and fragmentation (NBER Working Paper No. 33309). National Bureau of Economic Research. https://doi.org/10.3386/w33309. Contribution: Formal economic coercion and integration–security trade-off, with sector concentration and substitute availability. Difference: The intended empirical innovation here is time-resolved technology and material adaptation with physical completion uncertainty, not simply reconfirming fragmentation costs. Use: core theoretical competitor.

Woods, D. (2026). The “black box” strategy: China's opacity signaling game in rare earths (REES). Asian Review of Political Economy, 5, Article 5. https://doi.org/10.1007/ s44216- 026- 00073-z. Contribution: Pooling/nondisclosure signaling and stochastic diversification simulation; simulation assumptions are explicitly illustrative. Difference: Present project constructs an auditable observable-policy index, estimates association with actual project transitions and does not treat hypothetical Monte Carlo probabilities as forecasts validated against completed plants. Use: closest opacity precedent; distinguish observable uncertainty from presumed intent.

Zou, B., Poncin, S., & Bertinelli, L. (2022). The U.S.–China supply competition for rare earth elements: A dynamic game view. Environmental Modeling & Assessment, 27, 883–900. https: //doi.org/10.1007/s10666- 022- 09819-4. Contribution: Published rare-earth resource-competition differential game, including open-loop and Markovian strategic behavior. Difference: The new game links different reciprocal chokepoints and estimated adaptation; it must not claim to be the first rare- earth differential game. Use: closest resource-game comparison, especially equilibrium concepts.

Liu, J., Rotemberg, M., & Traiberman, S. (2026). Sabotage as industrial policy. The Economic Journal, Advance online publication, Article ueag111. https:// doi.org/10.1093/ej/ueag111. Contribution: Formal conditions under which foreign productivity impairment can have non-monotone terms-of-trade and welfare effects. Difference: Reciprocal future adaptation and the destruction of coercive leverage over time, rather than only the contemporaneous industrial-policy welfare consequence. Use: theory positioning and caution on treating restrictions as automatically good or bad. 13.2 Semiconductor adaptation: disagreement is substantive

Anwar, S., Hu, B., Luan, Q., & Wang, K. (2024). Export controls and innovation performance: Unravelling the complex relationship between blacklisted Chinese firms and U.S. suppli- ers. The World Economy, 47 (7), 2995–3033. https://doi.org/10.1111/twec.13570. Contribution: Matching/difference-in-differences evidence of innovation responses among blacklisted Chinese firms and impacts on U.S. suppliers. Limit: Innovation indicators and treatment selection do not automatically demonstrate qualified substitution at leading technology layers. Data caveat: underlying CSMAR data subject to license per publisher.

Hu, H., Yang, S., Zeng, L., & Zhang, X. (2024). U.S.–China trade conflicts and R&D investment: Evidence from the BIS entity lists. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 11, Article 829. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599- 024- 03369-8. Contribution: Firm R&D/input response to restrictions. Limit: R&D is not functioning semiconductor capability. Action: confirm exact authors/metadata and its effect definitions with publisher PDF before final manuscript.

Hayakawa, K., & Yang, C.-H. (2026). Technology sanctions and firm R&D: Evidence from the U.S.–China trade dispute. Economics & Politics, 38(2), 406–419. https://doi.org/10.1111/ec po.70033. Contribution: A matching analysis that does not find a significant positive R&D increase for treated firms. Interpretation: sign of induced effort must be estimated rather than structurally as- sumed positive. Limit: Firm-level sample and R&D do not directly measure foundry yield or equipment qualification. 13.3 Investment uncertainty, project duration and causal designs

Bloom, N. (2009). The impact of uncertainty shocks. Econometrica, 77 (3), 623– 685. https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA6248. Use: macro uncertainty/shock controls; not itself a measure of strategic nondisclosure.

Gulen, H., & Ion, M. (2016). Policy uncertainty and corporate investment. The Review of Financial Studies, 29(3), 523–564. https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhv050. Use: irreversibil- ity/uncertainty and investment response; retain confounding risks when applying to REEs.

Handley, K., & Limão, N. (2015). Trade and investment under policy uncertainty: Theory and firm evidence. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 7 (4), 189–222. https: //doi.org/10.1257/pol.20140068. Use: trade-policy uncertainty and firm investment; check the transfer from tariff uncertainty to licensing ambiguity.

Dixit, A. K., & Pindyck, R. S. (1994). Investment under uncertainty. Princeton University Press. Use: real-option delay intuition. Limit: no direct rare-earth project-hazard parameter estimated in this book.

Cox, D. R. (1972). Regression models and life-tables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 34(2), 187–202. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1972.tb00899 .x. Use: cause-specific duration-model robustness, proportional-hazards diagnostics.

Fine, J. P., & Gray, R. J. (1999). A proportional hazards model for the sub- distribution of a competing risk. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 94(446), 496–509. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1999.10474144. Use: cumulative incidence robustness when cancel- lation competes with commissioning; not a substitute for the full transition simulator.

Callaway, B., & Sant'Anna, P. H. C. (2021). Difference-in-differences with multiple time periods. Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 200–230. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.12. 001. Use: heterogeneous cohort-specific treatment effects.

Sun, L., & Abraham, S. (2021). Estimating dynamic treatment effects in event studies with heterogeneous treatment effects. Journal of Econometrics, 225(2), 175–199. https://doi. org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.09.006. Use: avoiding misleading TWFE event-time averages.

Callaway, B., Goodman-Bacon, A., & Sant'Anna, P. H. C. (2024). Difference-in-differences with a continuous treatment (NBER Working Paper No. 32117). https: //doi.org/10.3386/w32117. Use: thinking about dose/exposure when a well-meaning continuous treat- ment measure is defensible. Ordinal rule category scores by themselves are not naturally continuous dosages.

Gneiting, T., & Raftery, A. E. (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 102(477), 359–378. https://doi.org/10 .1198/016214506000001437. Use: CRPS/log-score/probability forecast calibration; explicit error score definition.

Brier, G. W. (1950). Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability. Monthly Weather Review, 78(1), 1–3. Use: binary forecast scoring; time-to-event scoring must address censoring. 13.4 Game theory, computation and nonlinear tipping

Maskin, E., & Tirole, J. (2001). Markov perfect equilibrium: I. Observable actions. Journal of Economic Theory, 100(2), 191–219. https://doi.org/10.1006/jeth.2000.2785. Use: equilibrium concepts; not a global existence theorem for the specialized continuous-state game.

Fink, A. M. (1964). Equilibrium in a stochastic n-person game. Journal of Science of the Hiroshima University, Series A-I, 28, 89–93. Use: stationary mixed equilibria in finite discounted stochastic games; the pure continuous feedback game remains conditional.

Pakes, A., & McGuire, P. (2001). Stochastic algorithms, symmetric Markov perfect equilibrium, and the “curse” of dimensionality. Econometrica, 69(5), 1261–1281. https://doi.org/10.1 111/1468-0262.00241. Use: computational caution and MPE methods.

Bardi, M., & Capuzzo-Dolcetta, I. (1997). Optimal control and viscosity solutions of Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations. Birkhäuser. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-8176-4755-1. Use: PDE/state constraint/upwinding mathematics. Verify edition metadata before final BibTeX.

Granovetter, M. (1978). Threshold models of collective behavior. American Journal of Sociology, 83(6), 1420–1443. https://doi.org/10.1086/226707. Use: individual adoption thresholds generating aggregate regimes; analogy, not data from mineral projects.

Watts, D. J. (2002). A simple model of global cascades on random networks. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 99(9), 5766–5771. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.082 090499. Use: distinguishes local cascade thresholds from ordinary physical loss propagation.

Schelling, T. C. (1971). Dynamic models of segregation. Journal of Mathematical Sociology, 1(2), 143–186. https://doi.org/10.1080/0022250X.1971.9989794. Use: path dependence and nonlinear collective composition; methodological analogy only.

Arthur, W. B. (1989). Competing technologies, increasing returns, and lock-in by historical events. The Economic Journal, 99(394), 116–131. https://doi.org/10.2307/2234208. Use: positive feedback and technological lock-in, motivating but not proving industrial REE tipping. 13.5 Oﬀicial baseline, legal instruments and data entries

International Energy Agency. (2026). Rare earth elements. https://ww w.iea.org/reports/rare- earth- elements/executive- summary. Use: primary chain taxonomy, 2024 production-concentration baselines, 2035 announced capacity comparators. Constraint: its pipeline is a forecast/scenario, not realized operating output.
